title: When the day goes wrong
hookLine: the rhythm isn't a test; start again at the next hour
tomorrow: a boy falls out of a window at church. why tell us that?

lines: I FELL. WHAT DO I DO NOW?
cards: The alarm never went off. No reading, no quiet minute, just keys, a sprint for the car, and a sharp word thrown over the shoulder on the way out.
By noon the whole shape looks broken, and a sensible voice offers a deal: write today off, start fresh Monday. An old story from the desert monks begins in exactly that spot.
A young monk walks out to an old one's cell and says it plainly: I fell. What do I do now?

teach.b: The old man's answer: get up again. The brother pushes. And if I fall again?
Get up again. The story, as the sayings keep it, never gives him a limit. It just keeps saying get up.
No lecture, no stricter rule, no new plan for next week. That sounds blunt until you hear it beside the Bible.

teach.h: A JUST MAN FALLETH, AND RISETH.
teach.b: Proverbs already expects the fall: “For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again.” The just person isn't the one with a clean record. It's the one who keeps rising.

teach.h: NEW EVERY MORNING, FROM THE RUBBLE.
teach.b: And Lamentations, a book of grief over a city in ruins, says this from the rubble, in the King James Bible: “It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.”
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: that line, which sounds like a greeting card, comes from the middle of a lament. Not after a good week. From the wreckage.
So a daily rhythm was never a test to pass or fail. Missing the morning doesn't cancel noon, and a sharp word at breakfast can still be mended by lunch.
The Monday plan sounds like discipline, but it quietly hands away the rest of today.
Start again doesn't wait for a new week. It waits for the next hour.

how: Christians who keep a daily rhythm of prayer often speak of simply picking it up again at the next hour after missing a time, and some say Lamentations 3:22–23 when they do.

games.q: what does “when the day goes wrong” mean?
o: a sign the routine was too strict and should be dropped
picking the rhythm back up at the next hour after a bad start
waiting for a clean new week before trying it all again

games.q: the fall and the rising — tap the pairs.
p: I fell. what do I do?
a just man falleth seven times

s: "great is thy faithfulness" comes from a happy song of thanks
it comes from Lamentations, grief over a city in ruins, said from the rubble.
Proverbs pictures the just person as someone who falls
a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again.
in the desert story, the old monk sets a limit on getting up
the brother asks again and again; the answer stays the same: get up again.

games.q: your friend's workout app reset her streak to zero after she missed Tuesday. she says she'll start over next month. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: go today: the fall is the place you get up from.
wait for next month, so the new streak starts clean.
double tomorrow's workout to make up the lost day.
games.why: Proverbs' just man falls and rises; the old monk said get up again, not wait for a clean start. the next hour is close enough.

practice: Say out loud, quietly, one thing that went wrong today, in a single sentence, with no defense attached.

Then say the very next small piece of your day, a breath, a line, a text that mends a sharp word, and begin it before the sit ends. If you pray, you can add Lamentations' words aloud: great is thy faithfulness.

wordCard.voice: When the day goes wrong. Not a verdict on the day, just a fall, and the next hour is close enough to get up in.

orig.note: the Hebrew for new in Lamentations 3:23: they are new every morning.

carryVoice: Your line: start again. Not next Monday; the next hour is soon enough. See you tomorrow.
